title: Is the Online Safety Act Making the Internet Safer?
label: 15 September 2026 · Online Safety Act and Ofcom
summary: The House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee questions Ofcom, the UK's online safety regulator, about whether the Online Safety Act is protecting children and holding technology companies accountable. Ofcom reports progress on age checks, restrictions on harmful websites and investigations into major platforms, but acknowledges that improvements in children's everyday online experiences have been disappointing so far. Committee members challenge Ofcom over slow enforcement, unpaid fines, legal loopholes and the difficulty of keeping pace with new technologies. The witnesses argue that the law provides a useful starting point but needs targeted changes, particularly to make companies address all the risks they identify, allow stronger action against persistent offenders and make it easier to require automatic detection of harmful material.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Baroness Keeley
speakers.role: Chair of the Communications and Digital Committee

speakers.label: Mark Bunting
speakers.name: Mark Bunting
speakers.role: Director, Online Safety Strategy Delivery, Ofcom

glossary.definition: The UK's communications regulator, responsible for enforcing the Online Safety Act.
A UK law passed in 2023 requiring online services to take steps to protect users, particularly children, from specified harms.
A review in which a company identifies the ways its service could harm users and considers how to reduce those risks.
Detailed guidance from Ofcom setting out measures companies can take to meet their legal online safety duties.
A legal protection under which companies following Ofcom's codes are treated as complying with the relevant duties, even if some risks remain.
A legal responsibility to take reasonable steps to protect people from foreseeable harm.
A court process that examines whether a public body's decision or action was lawful.
Court orders that can restrict access to an online service in the UK or interfere with its ability to operate.
A virtual private network, which can disguise a user's location and sometimes allow them to bypass website restrictions.
Artificial intelligence: computer technology that can perform tasks such as generating text, images and other material.
A set of computer instructions that, on social media, can determine which posts, videos or other material users are shown.
The UK government department responsible for public finances, including money collected through regulatory fines.

chapters.title: 1. When Will the Law Be Fully in Force?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom expects the original law to be fully implemented by mid-2027, but new government plans could affect that timetable unless extra resources are provided.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Online Safety Act was passed in 2023 and made Ofcom responsible for regulating online safety. Which parts are now in force, and what's still to come?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: There are three main parts: protecting people from illegal material, protecting children from certain harmful material even when it's legal, and imposing extra requirements on the largest or most influential services. The first two sets of duties came into force during 2025. Companies now have legal responsibilities that we can enforce.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The third part has taken longer, partly because Wikimedia challenged the process for deciding which services should face the extra rules. We've since published the list of services covered and consulted on those requirements. We currently expect them all to take effect by mid-2027.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We're also implementing newer requirements, including offences relating to cyberstalking and serious health harm. Later this year we'll propose rules requiring certain intimate images shared without consent to be removed within 48 hours.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Government is now planning a social media ban for under-16s. What will that mean for your timetable?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We already had a full workload before that announcement. We've moved staff onto the proposed ban, but without extra people and funding, other work will have to be delayed. The Government promised additional funding in June, and we're discussing our plans with it. We think we can deliver everything if the work is properly funded and scheduled.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What have you learned from implementing the first stages of the Act?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We moved quickly because we wanted protections in place. But that meant consulting companies, campaigners and experts before we'd gathered as much evidence as we'd have liked. We've since learned to involve them more effectively. Our guidance on protecting women and girls benefited from that, and we're using a similar approach to decide what information major platforms should publish about their safety practices.

chapters.title: 2. Are Children Actually Safer?
chapters.takeaway: Age checks and other safeguards have spread, but Ofcom admits that evidence of meaningful improvements in children's everyday online experiences remains limited.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner told us she'd asked to see companies' risk assessments and that Ofcom refused. Why wouldn't you share information about the dangers companies have identified?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We've worked closely with the Commissioner, but we haven't received a formal request for those assessments. Under the Act, we need a company's consent before sharing its information with someone else. If she makes a formal request, we'll approach the companies and ask whether they agree.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That's surprising, because she told us she'd already asked and been refused.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: There have been discussions between our teams for months, but not a formal request. We're willing to follow the legal process for sharing the information.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Let's get to the fundamental question. Has the Act actually made children and adults safer online?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We've seen significant changes in companies' behaviour. In a survey of 125 businesses, 76% said they'd completed a risk assessment, 44% said they'd changed their services to meet the law, and 59% believed they'd implemented its requirements fully or substantially. But the Act covers around 100,000 services, so this is only part of the picture.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The most visible change is age checking. Since the requirements began in July 2025, major services including Reddit, X and Discord have introduced checks. All 10 of the largest pornography sites now have them. Among the 100 largest, around three-quarters have either introduced checks or blocked UK users. In a sample of 32 companies, the number of age checks increased 23-fold. We believe that has substantially reduced children's access to pornography.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Some harmful services have stopped allowing UK access altogether, including a prominent suicide forum and websites associated with child sexual abuse material. But we're less satisfied with the biggest platforms children use. X has made commitments about removing hateful and terrorist material faster, while Meta and Snap have promised changes to tackle adults grooming children. We need to see those promises produce results.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: The Children's Commissioner told us the Act has made absolutely no difference. How do you respond to that?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I share her frustration. We're trying to change how companies operate, including the decisions their leaders make about safety. Some of those companies have worked in the same way for decades. Changing that takes time, though I recognise that people want improvements now. When we measure the overall effect so far, we've been disappointed too.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's not enough for a company to introduce one safety feature. Some platforms have promised to make it harder for strangers to contact children, but we're not yet convinced they can reliably identify which users are children. Without that, the protection may not work properly.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Should companies be allowed to operate if they can't guarantee children's safety? Could you ultimately stop a social media platform operating in the UK?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Act makes companies legally responsible for taking safety measures, though it doesn't guarantee that every risk disappears. If a company breaks the law and won't put things right, we can seek a court order restricting its access to the UK. That wouldn't shut it down internationally.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You're hearing from children through the Children's Commissioner. Is there evidence that their actual experiences online have improved?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: There's encouraging evidence from individual accounts, and we're collecting more systematic information. But it's a complicated picture. AI has also made some dangers worse, including making child sexual abuse material easier to create and distribute. I believe the Act is helping, but we're dealing with harmful technologies that are developing rapidly.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: What about gaming? Have you made progress protecting children there?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: We've focused mainly on how players interact, particularly when adults may try to contact children. On platforms such as Roblox, we've pushed for age checks and protections against unwanted contact. Some gaming services, including Xbox and Steam, have introduced age checks. But broader questions, such as violent games and excessive screen time, aren't generally covered by our current duties. Social media has also been a higher priority.

chapters.title: 3. The Loophole in the Safety Rules
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says companies can sometimes follow its detailed rules while leaving serious dangers unresolved, creating pressure for a stronger responsibility to address risks.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: You've raised concerns about something called the safe harbour. Would you like that removed from the Online Safety Act?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's complicated. Companies must assess the risks their services create, but the law also provides codes of practice explaining what they should do. Under the safe harbour, a company that follows those codes is treated as meeting its legal duties, even if its own assessment shows that serious risks remain. We can ask it voluntarily to do more, but we may not be able to compel it.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: The advantage is certainty. Companies know what they're expected to do, and it's easier for us to prove they've broken a clear rule. I'd like companies to have to address all the risks they identify, even if that means going beyond our codes. But enforcing a broad requirement to take every reasonable precaution could lead to lengthy legal arguments about what's reasonable.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Campaigners have suggested a duty of care instead, meaning companies would be responsible for designing products that don't harm users. Wouldn't that be easier to enforce?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Not necessarily. I don't think the main problem is the requirement that safety measures be proportionate. It's the way the safe harbour works and the fact that the law requires us to specify clear, detailed steps. That puts too much responsibility on Ofcom to identify every necessary precaution, instead of making companies work out how to address the dangers on their own services.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: A duty of care is an alternative worth considering, but we'd still need to define what it meant for a huge range of companies, including very small ones. Major platforms already have sophisticated safety systems, yet those systems may not prevent enough harm. They can argue strongly that they've followed our codes and therefore can't be forced to do more. That's a real enforcement problem.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Shouldn't online services be safe by design, particularly when children use them? What does that mean in practice?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It means companies should build their services to prevent harm as far as reasonably possible, rather than waiting for problems and removing individual posts afterwards. That's already central to our approach. We focus on how services are designed, how users interact and what safety systems companies put in place. But we can't remove every risk, and the safe harbour limits how far we can push companies beyond our existing rules.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: The Molly Rose Foundation says teenagers' exposure to dangerous material about suicide, self-harm, depression and eating disorders has barely changed. That's a serious criticism. What's preventing you from doing more, faster?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: One problem is detecting harmful material before anyone sees it. Companies can act after users report something, or they can use automatic tools to find and remove it first. The second approach is preferable, but we don't yet have enough evidence about how well companies' existing tools work. We're consulting on requiring wider use of them.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: There's a difficult balance. These tools can involve scanning everything users upload, which raises concerns about privacy and freedom of expression. Parliament therefore set conditions requiring us to establish that they're accurate and effective before making companies use them. We think there's a strong case for wider use, but we need to demonstrate it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fleet
turns.text: That sounds like a fundamental weakness in the law.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It may be an area needing change. We do think it's right to examine the consequences carefully before requiring companies to scan everyone's material. But these tools could be crucial to preventing the harms you've described, and we're developing proposals.

chapters.title: 4. Is Ofcom Acting Quickly Enough?
chapters.takeaway: Committee members accuse Ofcom of moving too slowly, while its officials point to investigations already under way and the legal difficulties of regulating powerful companies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Campaigners say Ofcom is slow, reactive and struggles to deal with new dangers. Why can't you respond more quickly when technology changes?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We can move quickly when a serious new problem appears. Take Grok, the AI tool on X. When concerns emerged about it generating illegal material around the start of this year, we launched an investigation within two weeks. We also gather information from police, campaigners and experts so we can identify problems as they emerge.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: There's a concern that you insist on proving a measure will work before you're willing to try it. Doesn't that leave you constantly behind?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We don't require absolute certainty before acting. But we're operating in an environment where companies frequently challenge us in court. Meta has brought judicial reviews over our fees, and other companies are challenging our requests for information or decisions about which services face extra rules. If we take unnecessary legal risks, well-funded companies can seriously obstruct our work. We have to balance speed with decisions that can survive those challenges.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: But the Molly Rose Foundation and the Children's Commissioner both say you're failing to get ahead of emerging harms. Why do so many people see you as too slow?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: The Act covers more than 100,000 services and around 140 priority offences. We can't tackle everything equally at once. We have to concentrate on particular harms where we think we can make a meaningful difference. Inevitably, that leaves other serious problems receiving less attention for now.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: People feel Ofcom simply isn't using its powers forcefully enough. Is that because the law restricts you, or because you're reluctant to confront these companies?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I agree that we need companies to believe we'll act and impose penalties that genuinely hurt. There's a perception problem, but I disagree that we haven't used our powers. This is a new regulatory system covering companies that have never faced this sort of oversight and often strongly resist it. We've concentrated initially on gathering information and enforcing clear requirements, while developing our approach to more complex cases.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We've opened six enforcement programmes and 40 formal investigations covering more than 100 services over the past 18 months. We've imposed £7 million in penalties. Our earlier cases often involved smaller sites with straightforward breaches, but we're now investigating major platforms, including X over Grok, Telegram over child sexual abuse material and TikTok. We're also starting to use powers that could make senior managers personally criminally liable.

chapters.title: 5. Why Fines and Website Blocking Can Fail
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom can investigate and fine companies, but unpaid penalties and restrictions on court-ordered blocking make enforcement difficult, especially against overseas websites.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: You said you'd run out of legal options against a US-based suicide forum. Doesn't that suggest the powers Parliament gave you are inadequate?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: There's certainly a problem with the powers for restricting websites. We've been very active compared with regulators in other countries, but these cases take time, and some of our investigations haven't reached a conclusion yet. We want to move faster.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: Many services are small, based overseas and have no money or property in the UK that we can easily pursue. Some haven't paid their fines. We're trying to recover the money, but getting a foreign court to recognise and enforce a UK penalty can be very difficult.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: There's another problem with business disruption measures, which let us seek court orders restricting services. We can apply only when a company is still breaking the law. The suicide forum stopped making its service available in the UK, so we could no longer pursue it under those powers, even though there were concerns about people accessing it by other means.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: We've also had pornography sites introduce proper age checks after enforcement action but then refuse to pay their fines. Once they've corrected the original breach, we can't seek a blocking order simply because the fine remains unpaid. Being able to do that would be very helpful.

turns.speaker: Viscount Colville of Culross
turns.text: Children can still use VPNs to disguise their location and get around restrictions. Australia is considering stronger requirements to prevent that. Should the UK law be changed?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: VPN use increased after age checks came in, but not so dramatically that we think huge numbers of people are bypassing the law. It could become a bigger issue. Whether companies should be required to block VPN access is a political decision for the Government and Parliament, not Ofcom.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Of the £7 million in fines you've imposed, how much have you actually collected?

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: I don't have the exact figure with me, but we can provide it. We received another payment this week. Realistically, though, the majority remains unpaid.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: That problem has been especially noticeable because our early fines involved smaller overseas sites. As we increasingly deal with major companies that have assets in the UK, I expect recovering penalties to become less of an issue.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: You've talked about changing corporate culture over time, but these industries move incredibly quickly. Don't we need tougher financial consequences? And could fines help fund the resources you need?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: We absolutely need financial pressure. Companies won't necessarily change voluntarily. As regulators and courts around the world take action, safety becomes a serious financial concern for company leaders, not just something their safety teams discuss. That's essential to changing their behaviour.

chapters.title: 6. VPNs, US Lawsuits and the Limits of the Act
chapters.takeaway: The committee explores whether stronger rules on VPNs and lessons from US legal action could improve UK protections, while Ofcom cautions against replacing the entire system.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: When Parliament was debating the Act, a Minister suggested that companies would have to account for children using VPNs to bypass age checks. Doesn't that mean companies should prevent this?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I don't think the Act requires companies to stop people using VPNs. We have taken action against companies that encourage people to use them to get around age restrictions, but that's different from a general obligation to block VPN access.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: What if a company can detect that someone's using a VPN? Shouldn't it refuse them access?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: That's a much bigger question. VPNs have many legitimate uses, including in workplaces. Requiring services to block them would be a significant change affecting far more than children's access to harmful material. Parliament and the Government would need to consider those consequences.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Meta has recently agreed to a substantial settlement in US legal proceedings. Does that change how much you think companies should be fined here?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: It certainly makes senior executives take online safety more seriously. But our fines are governed by UK law, which allows penalties of up to 10% of a company's qualifying worldwide revenue. We have our own process for deciding the appropriate amount, rather than following the figure in a US settlement.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: And to answer the earlier funding question, Ofcom doesn't keep those fines. They go to the Treasury. Our online safety work is now funded through charges on the companies we regulate.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: What's interesting about the Meta settlement is its focus on how platforms are designed, rather than simply individual harmful posts. Does that suggest our law is missing something?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: Many of the settlement's protections, such as preventing harmful contact between adults and children, are already consistent with our rules. The main difference is that it also addresses features that encourage people to spend excessive amounts of time on a platform. The Online Safety Act doesn't generally regulate screen time or addictive design. Parliament discussed those issues but didn't include them.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Should we add them? And could the same commitments be required of Meta and other platforms in the UK?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: Those are ultimately decisions for government and Parliament. The Government is considering measures such as a social media ban and restrictions on when children can use platforms. The Meta agreement also only covers a set period, rather than requiring the changes forever. We can't enforce requirements beyond the powers Parliament has given us, but we can strongly encourage companies to adopt protections here that they've agreed to elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Lord Knight of Weymouth
turns.text: Could it be more effective to hold platforms legally responsible for harm to individuals, as happens in some US cases, rather than concentrating on whether they've followed detailed regulatory rules? Should we replace those rules with a broader duty of care?

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I'd be cautious about replacing the whole system so early. The UK doesn't have the same tradition of large group lawsuits as the US, so the results might be different. There are specific improvements we could make, but the underlying principle is sound: companies should have legal responsibilities to protect users, with strong incentives to meet them. We're still in the early stages of making that work.

chapters.title: 7. Three Changes Ofcom Wants
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses identify three priorities: making companies address all known risks, strengthening website-blocking powers and allowing wider use of technology that detects harmful material before users see it.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: I'd like each of you to identify the single change to the Online Safety Act that would most improve your ability to protect people online.

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: I'd focus on making companies take responsibility for all the risks they've identified in their assessments, rather than simply following our codes of practice. That would give us more scope to challenge major platforms about dangers they know exist but haven't adequately addressed.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: Australia has considered legislation based on a digital duty of care. Could that approach work here?

turns.speaker: Mark Bunting
turns.text: It's one model worth examining, but we'd have to work out carefully how it would fit alongside the existing Act. I wouldn't present it as a quick fix.

turns.speaker: Suzanne Cater
turns.text: My priority is fixing the business disruption measures. They're our strongest enforcement powers, but we've found major practical obstacles to using them. Changes that made court-ordered restrictions more workable would make a real difference. We're happy to give the committee more detail in writing.

turns.speaker: Oliver Griffiths
turns.text: I'd make it easier for us to require companies to use technology that automatically identifies harmful content before it reaches users. That would give platforms more ability, and responsibility, to prevent people being exposed to dangerous material in the first place.
